prompt: `Book` declares no `describe()`. Why does `book.describe()` compile and run?
hint: What does `extends Item` give `Book`?

choices.text: `Book` inherits it from `Item`, which `extends` made its superclass
choices.why: Right: a subclass has every method its superclass has.

choices.text: The compiler copies `describe()` into `Book.class`
choices.why: `javap -p Book` showed no `describe()` in `Book.class`; it is found in `Item` when called.

choices.text: Every class gets a `describe()` from `java.lang.Object`
choices.why: `Object` gives `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode`, not `describe`.

prompt: `describe()` is written once, in `Item`, and calls `loanDays()`. Why does the DVD's line say 7 days and the book's 14?
hint: Which `loanDays()` exists on a `Dvd` object?

choices.text: `describe()` checks whether the item is a `Dvd` before choosing the number
choices.why: There is no check in `describe()`; it just calls `loanDays()`.

choices.text: `Dvd` overrides `loanDays()`, and the call runs the version of the object it is made on
choices.why: Right: on a DVD the overriding `loanDays()` runs; lesson 25 explains how.

choices.text: Because `Dvd`'s constructor passes 7 to `super`
choices.why: The constructor passes a title and a year; the 7 comes from a method.

choices.text: `@Override` copies the new value into `Item`
choices.why: `@Override` asks for a check and changes nothing in `Item`.

prompt: With `super(title, year);` removed from `Book`'s constructor, the compiler said `required: String,int`, `found: no arguments`. What had it done?
hint: A constructor always starts with a call to another one.

choices.text: Looked for a `Book()` constructor with no arguments
choices.why: The message names `Item`'s constructor, not `Book`'s.

choices.text: Inserted a call to `super()` with no arguments, which `Item` cannot accept
choices.why: Right: with no explicit call, an argument-less `super()` is inserted, and `Item` has no such constructor.

choices.text: Refused because `title` and `year` were never assigned
choices.why: Unassigned fields would be a different error; this one is about a constructor call.

prompt: `Book.author()` tried to read `year`, which `Item` declares `private`. What happened?
hint: A book has a year. May its code touch it?

choices.text: It compiled, because a subclass sees everything its superclass declares
choices.why: It did not: `private` is private to the declaring class, subclasses included.

choices.text: It compiled and printed 0, because the subclass gets its own empty copy
choices.why: There is one `year`, set by `Item`'s constructor; the compiler refused the read.

choices.text: A compile error: `year has private access in Item`
choices.why: Right: `protected` would have opened it; `private` did not.

prompt: The modifier that lets a subclass read a field its superclass declares, as `Item` does with `title`, is ___.
hint: Between private and public.

prompt: Inside `Dvd.describe()`, `super.describe()` runs `Item`'s version. Which `loanDays()` does that version call?
hint: `super` picks a method, not an object.

choices.text: `Item`'s, because `super` switches the whole call to the parent
choices.why: The line printed 7 days, which is `Dvd`'s `loanDays()`.

choices.text: `Dvd`'s: the object is still the DVD
choices.why: Right: `super` chose which `describe()` ran, and the object stayed a DVD.

choices.text: Neither: a method called through `super` cannot call others
choices.why: It called `loanDays()` and the result appeared in the line.

prompt: What is the superclass of `Item`, which declares none?
hint: `Chain` printed it.

choices.text: None: `getSuperclass()` returns `null` for it
choices.why: `null` came after `java.lang.Object`, the parent of `Item`.

choices.text: `java.lang.Object`, the root every class sits under
choices.why: Right: a class that does not say `extends` extends `Object`.

choices.text: `Book`, since it is the first class to extend `Item`
choices.why: The arrow goes the other way: `Book` extends `Item`.

prompt: Two `Book` objects with the same title, year and author: why is `a.equals(b)` false?
hint: Which class wrote the `equals` that ran?

choices.text: Because `equals` compares the hash codes, and those differ
choices.why: `Object.equals` compares identity directly; the hash codes differing is a second symptom.

choices.text: Because `author` is private, so `equals` cannot compare it
choices.why: Object's `equals` compares no fields at all, private or not.

choices.text: `Book` inherits `Object.equals`, which is the same as `==`
choices.why: Right: two different objects, so false, until a class overrides `equals` and `hashCode`.

prompt: `System.out.println(a)` printed `Book@7ad041f3`. Run the program again and what changes?
hint: The number is derived from the object's identity.

choices.text: Nothing: it is the book's position in memory, which is fixed
choices.why: It is derived from identity, and it differs on every run.

choices.text: The number after `@`
choices.why: Right: `Object.toString` prints a value tied to that object's identity, which is new on every run.

choices.text: The class name, if `Book` is compiled again
choices.why: The class name comes from the class and stays `Book`.

choices.text: It prints the title instead, once the object has been used
choices.why: `toString` prints the same shape until a class overrides it.

prompt: Match each method inherited from `Object` to what its default does.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.right: Class name, `@`, and a number from the object's identity
True only for the very same object
A number derived from the object's identity

right_distractors: Compares every field of the two objects

prompt: What did the compiler say about `public class Book extends Item, Dvd`?
hint: It expected the class body.

choices.text: `'{' expected`, at the comma
choices.why: Right: single inheritance is a rule of the grammar.

choices.text: That `Dvd` and `Item` both declare `loanDays()`
choices.why: It never got that far; the error was at the comma.

choices.text: Nothing: it compiled, and `Book` took `Dvd`'s methods
choices.why: It refused; a class extends exactly one class.

prompt: Which of these passes the is-a test for `extends`?
hint: Say the sentence: every X is a Y.

choices.text: `Loan extends Book`, since a loan needs a book's title
choices.why: A loan has a book; that is a field.

choices.text: `Member extends HashSet<String>`, to keep a member's ISBNs
choices.why: A member is not a set; the set belongs in a field.

choices.text: `Magazine extends Item`
choices.why: Right: a magazine is something the library lends, with a title and a year.

choices.text: `Item extends Book`, so items get an author
choices.why: Not every item is a book; a DVD would get an author it does not have.

prompt: `CountingSet` was given three ISBNs in one `addAll`. What count did it report?
hint: Each one was counted twice.

prompt: Why did `CountingSet` count each ISBN twice, when neither of its methods is wrong on its own?
hint: What does `HashSet.addAll` do inside?

choices.text: `List.of` hands each element over twice, once per method that adds
choices.why: `size()` was 3: the list had three elements and the set three.

choices.text: `addAll` calls `add` inside, and `add` is overridden too
choices.why: Right: a detail of how `HashSet` is written, which the subclass came to depend on.

choices.text: `@Override` makes each overriding method run twice
choices.why: `@Override` only asks for a check; it runs nothing.

choices.text: The counter is shared by the set and its superclass
choices.why: There is one `added` field, in `CountingSet`; it was incremented twice per ISBN.

prompt: `CountingShelf` reported 3 for the same three ISBNs. What made it immune to `HashSet`'s internals?
hint: It has a set; it is not one.

choices.text: It calls `add` in a loop, which `HashSet` does not
choices.why: `HashSet.addAll` also calls `add`; the difference is whose `add`.

choices.text: It keeps the set in a field, out of `HashSet`'s reach
choices.why: Right: composition; the set is used only through its public methods.

choices.text: Its field is `private`, which stops `HashSet` from double-counting
choices.why: Visibility of the field is not what changed the count; who calls whom is.

prompt: Put the classes in order from the root of the hierarchy down to the class `Lending` created.
hint: `Chain` printed them the other way round.

prompt: A `Book` object has which of these, without `Book.java` declaring them? Choose all that apply.
hint: Everything from `Item` and from `Object`.

choices.text: `loanDays()`
choices.why: Yes: inherited from `Item`.

choices.text: `hashCode()`
choices.why: Yes: inherited from `Object`, through `Item`.

choices.text: a `year` field, though its code cannot read it
choices.why: Yes: the object has it, set by `Item`'s constructor; `private` stops `Book`'s code reading it.

choices.text: a `minutes` field
choices.why: That is `Dvd`'s; siblings share nothing but their parent.

prompt: You need a `Catalogue` that holds books and can be searched by author. A colleague proposes `Catalogue extends ArrayList<Book>`. What does the lesson say?
hint: Say the sentence, then think about `CountingSet`.

choices.text: Good: a catalogue is a list, and it inherits `add` and `get` for free
choices.why: It inherits every list method, including ones that bypass any rule the catalogue keeps, and ties it to `ArrayList`'s internals.

choices.text: Keep the list in a private field; offer only what a catalogue needs
choices.why: Right: composition keeps `ArrayList`'s details out of `Catalogue`'s behaviour.

choices.text: Extend `Book` instead, since a catalogue is made of books
choices.why: A catalogue is not a book; that fails the is-a test outright.

prompt: Where may `super(...)` appear in a constructor, in the code this lesson wrote?
hint: The item part is built before the book part.

choices.text: Anywhere, as long as it is called once
choices.why: The superclass part must exist before the subclass part uses it.

choices.text: Only in classes that extend something other than `Object`
choices.why: Every constructor calls a superclass constructor, `Object`'s included; it is just inserted for you.

choices.text: As the first thing, before `this.author = author`
choices.why: Right: lesson 27 shows the statements Java 25 allows before it, and what they may not touch.

prompt: Holding an object in a field and using its public methods, instead of extending its class, is called ___.
hint: `CountingShelf` does it.
